title: dynamic blocks and lifecycle rules
summary: Generate repeated nested blocks with dynamic, and control how Terraform replaces things: create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, ignore_changes and replace_triggered_by.

steps.title: dynamic: repeated nested blocks from data
body: Some resources take repeated **nested blocks**: `ingress` rules in a security group, `setting` blocks in an Elastic
Beanstalk environment, `source` blocks in an archive. `count` and `for_each` repeat whole resources; `dynamic`
description = ingress.key             # the iterator is named after the block
Use it when the blocks really come from data (a variable, a map). Do not use it to save typing two fixed blocks:
readers then have to run the loop in their head to know what is deployed.

steps.title: One release zip, driven by a map
prompt: `~/infra/release/main.tf` builds the release zip with `data "archive_file"` and three hand-written `source` blocks
that repeat what `local.release_files` already says. Every release, someone forgets one of the two places.
1. Replace the three `source` blocks with one `dynamic "source"` over `local.release_files` (file name to content).
2. Add a fourth file to the map: `RELEASE_NOTES.md` with the content `Faster checkout\n`.
3. Apply, and check the zip: `unzip -l out/release.zip`.

checks.name: the zip has the four files
the notes are right
checks.fail: `RELEASE_NOTES.md` in the zip should contain `Faster checkout`.

checks.name: one dynamic block, driven by the map
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/release && grep -q 'dynamic "source"' main.tf && test "$(grep -cE '^ *source *\{' main.tf)" = 0 && grep -q 'local.release_files' main.tf
checks.fail: `main.tf` should have one `dynamic "source"` block with `for_each = local.release_files`, and no hand-written `source { }` blocks.

checks.name: applied
checks.fail: Apply, so the `release_sha256` output is up to date: `terraform plan` should show no changes.

hints: In `content { }`, `source.key` is the file name and `source.value` its content: `filename = source.key`, `content = source.value`.
Add `"RELEASE_NOTES.md" = "Faster checkout\n"` to the map, then `terraform plan -out=tfplan` and `terraform apply tfplan`.
steps.explain: Now the map is the only list of files. The same pattern builds security group rules from a variable, or Lambda layers from a list. An optional block is a `dynamic` with `for_each = var.enable_logging ? [1] : []`.

steps.title: lifecycle: how and whether things are replaced
body: create_before_destroy = true   # the new one exists before the old is deleted: no gap (+/- in the plan)
prevent_destroy = true          # any plan that would destroy (or replace) it fails
ignore_changes  = [engine_version]   # minor upgrades are applied by AWS itself
replace_triggered_by = [time_rotating.api_key]   # a new key whenever the rotation timer rolls over
Know their limits. `create_before_destroy` needs names that can exist twice (use `name_prefix`). `prevent_destroy`
only protects while the block exists: delete the block and the protection goes with it, so also turn on the
provider's own protection (`deletion_protection = true` on databases). `ignore_changes` hides drift on that

steps.prompt: A certificate on a live load balancer must be replaced (its domain list changed). With the default lifecycle, what does the apply do, and what fixes it?
options: It deletes the old certificate first, which fails or leaves the listener without one; `create_before_destroy = true` creates the new one first
It updates the certificate in place; nothing to fix
It creates both at once; `prevent_destroy` fixes it
It refuses to replace certificates; `ignore_changes` fixes it
steps.explain: The default for a replacement is destroy-then-create (`-/+`). With `create_before_destroy`, the plan shows `+/-`: create the new certificate, move the listener to it, then delete the old one. Anything referenced by something that must never be without it is a candidate.

steps.title: Protect the CA, rotate the API key
prompt: `~/infra/certs` holds the internal CA's key and a partner API key. Two findings from the security review:
1. **The CA key must never be destroyed by Terraform**, not even by a careless `terraform destroy` or a change that
would replace it. Add the right lifecycle rule. Prove it: `terraform plan -destroy` must fail.
2. **The partner API key must rotate every 90 days.** Add a `time_rotating` resource (`hashicorp/time`) with
`rotation_days = 90`, and make `random_password.partner_api_key` be replaced whenever it rotates.
Apply. The CA key must still be the same key afterwards.

checks.name: destroying the CA key is refused
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/certs && ! terraform plan -destroy -input=false -no-color > /tmp/d 2>&1 && grep -q 'Instance cannot be destroyed' /tmp/d && grep -q 'tls_private_key.ca' /tmp/d
checks.fail: `terraform plan -destroy` should fail with *Instance cannot be destroyed* for `tls_private_key.ca`. Add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` to it.

checks.name: a 90-day rotation timer exists
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/certs && t=$(terraform state list | grep '^time_rotating\.' | head -n1) && test -n "$t" && terraform state show -no-color "$t" | grep -Eq 'rotation_days *= *90'
checks.fail: The state should have a `time_rotating` resource with `rotation_days = 90`. Add it and apply.

checks.name: rotation replaces the API key
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/certs && t=$(terraform state list | grep '^time_rotating\.' | head -n1) && terraform plan -input=false -no-color -replace="$t" | grep -q 'random_password.partner_api_key will be replaced'
checks.fail: When the timer is replaced (`terraform plan -replace=time_rotating.<name>`), `random_password.partner_api_key` must be replaced too. Use `replace_triggered_by`.

checks.name: the CA key survived
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/certs && terraform state show -no-color tls_private_key.ca | grep -q "$(cat /opt/dojo/state/ca)" && terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -input=false -no-color >/dev/null
checks.fail: The CA key changed, or the plan is not clean. Apply your changes; nothing should replace the CA key.

hints: `resource "time_rotating" "partner_api_key" { rotation_days = 90 }`, and in the password: `lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [time_rotating.partner_api_key] }`.
Plan and apply (the new timer is created; read whether the key changes now), then `terraform plan -destroy` to see the protection.
solution: sed -i '/^  special = false$/a\  lifecycle {\n    replace_triggered_by = [time_rotating.partner_api_key]\n  }' main.tf
steps.explain: `time_rotating` stores a rotation time; once that time has passed, the next plan replaces it, and `replace_triggered_by` replaces the key with it. A scheduled pipeline run (daily `plan`/`apply`) is what actually rotates. `prevent_destroy` makes even `terraform destroy` fail for the whole configuration: that is the point, and also why it belongs on a few critical things only.

steps.prompt: Match the need to the lifecycle setting.
pairs: no gap while a certificate is replaced
a plan that would delete the database must fail
restart the app when its config changes
